## claude.ai NPI Registry
An MCP server for accessing the CMS NPPES NPI Registry API v2.1.

This server provides tools to validate, lookup, and search healthcare providers in the
United States National Plan and Provider Enumeration System (NPPES).

ABOUT THE NPI:
The National Provider Identifier (NPI) is a unique 10-digit identifier assigned to healthcare
providers in the United States. There are two types:
- NPI-1 (Individual): Physicians, nurses, dentists, pharmacists, therapists, etc.
- NPI-2 (Organization): Hospitals, clinics, pharmacies, laboratories, nursing homes, etc.

IMPORTANT LIMITATIONS:
- This registry only contains US healthcare providers
- Issuance of an NPI does NOT ensure the provider is licensed or credentialed
- International providers will NOT appear in this database
- API returns maximum 200 results per request, up to 1,200 total across paginated requests
- Data is updated daily from NPPES but may lag behind real-time changes

TOOL SELECTION GUIDE:
• npi_validate: Check NPI format + Luhn check digit (instant, no API call). Use FIRST before any lookup to catch typos.
• npi_lookup: Get full provider details by NPI number. Returns credentials, practice address, specialty, license.
• npi_search: Find providers by name, location, specialty, organization. Returns compact list with pagination support.

Physicians:
• 'Internal Medicine'
• 'Family Practice' / 'Family Med*'
• 'Cardiology' / 'Cardiovascular*'
• 'Oncology' / 'Hematology*'
• 'Neurology'
• 'Orthopedic Surgery'
• 'Psychiatry'
• 'Dermatology'
• 'Radiology'
• 'Emergency Medicine'

Hospitals & Facilities:
• 'General Acute Care Hospital'
• 'Pharmacy'
• 'Clinical Laboratory'
• 'Skilled Nursing Facility'
• 'Home Health Agency'
• 'Ambulatory Surgical Center'
• 'Urgent Care'
• 'Rehabilitation Hospital'
• 'Dialysis Center'

# Proposal Follow-Up — Scope, Costs & Jose's Technical Questions

*Hey team, this is in response to Nathan's follow-up (Shay, Jose, Diva cc'd). This answers everything raised and level-sets what the MVP is (and isn't) before kickoff. Would rather give more information and over communicate than not. Thanks, y’all!*

## The short version

We love the energy and we're aligned on moving forward. Almost everything in the follow-up is the *right destination* — a unified client database, SSO, role-based tiers, audit logs, scale architecture. The thing we want to make sure we're all holding together before kickoff is this:

**This first build is an MVP.** Its job is to give the account-manager role a genuinely 10x experience and to be *instrumented* so we can measure what's working and learn what AMs actually need next. 

The point of v1 is the feedback loop — not shipping the full org-wide platform on day one. The enterprise-grade items are where this goes; the MVP is how we earn the right to build them on real usage instead of guesses.

Nothing below is a no. It's a *when*.

## One thing worth saying up front: the R&D is already done — on us

Before the details, context that should make everyone more confident going in. Standing up something like this normally starts with a discovery-and-R&D phase (figuring out the architecture, testing what's actually possible, finding the dead ends)…. and that phase is usually billed, because it's real work and real risk. Most firms charge for it before a single feature exists.

We didn't do that. We've already spent the equivalent of this project's budget (and then some) doing that R&D ourselves, ahead of time and at our own cost. The architecture below isn't a theory we're going to go figure out on your dime; it's the result of work we've *already done*. That's why we can hand you a concrete, phased implementation plan instead of a “we'll scope it as we go.”

What that means for DR: you're not paying us to learn. You're paying us to *execute a plan that already exists… w*hich means we hit the ground running on day one, and the discovery risk that usually sits on the client's side of the table is already absorbed. This isn’t a pat on the back by any means… but because it's the reason this budget goes as far as it does and why the timeline is realistic rather than hopeful.

## What the MVP actually delivers

A tool your account managers log into (via Okta → “our” Digital Resource’s owned MCP) that gives the AM role a set of skills they can drive in natural language. It's built around the AM workflow and scoped for your AM team:

- **Website builds** — end-to-end Webflow sites: strategy, customer personas, competitive analysis, ~12 pages built out, blog content generated. Designer or AM can drop in a template (theirs or one of DR's existing templates). After v1, the AM keeps tweaking — add a blog page, change the footer, spin up a new page with new content. The basics, on demand.
    - *This is a very fun part for us because Webflow doesn’t even offer this to their end users as of today. First-mover energy for us.*
- **SEO** — build preliminary SEO work, then modify and iterate against their own strategy.
- **Ads** — create Google and Meta ads, pull performance data back, and build strategies/plans off it.
- **Reporting** — auto-pull and assemble client reports. This is the one we're most excited about: it replaces the 1–2 days AMs currently spend gathering Basecamp data and writing reports by hand.
- **Client handoff** — when a new AM picks up a client, they get a clean preliminary download of exactly what's happening on that account.

Under the hood, every action is instrumented so we get **success-rate evaluations** on each skill, plus visibility into what AMs are asking for that the tool *can't* do yet. That's the roadmap engine. This provides us ***a very light weight*** version to answer questions like:

- Which skills are AMs actually reaching for, and which are collecting dust?
- How much time is each skill giving back per AM per week?
- Are AMs returning to a skill after first use, or trying it once and abandoning it?
- Which outputs do AMs ship as-is vs. heavily edit before using? (Edit-rate is your real quality signal, not just "did it run.")
- What are AMs asking the tool to do that it *can't* yet? (The gap list = your roadmap, ranked by demand.)
- Which capability, if we built it next, would unlock the most AM time?
- What's worth building in-house vs. leaving to an off-the-shelf tool?

## The phased build plan (more laymans terms)

This is how we'd run it. Sequenced the way mature AI builds are run: foundation first, prove value, then harden and scale. Each phase has a job, a deliverable, and an **exit gate.** We don't move to the next phase until the current one clears its gate. That's how we keep the budget honest and avoid the classic failure mode where an AI project quietly balloons into an enterprise platform nobody asked for. 

<aside>
🤝

The principle the whole industry now converges on and what we follow suit on:
**Prove value on real usage before you spend to scale.**

</aside>

### Phase 0 — Foundation: Okta SSO & Authentication

*The job:* stand up the front door before anything else exists. Nothing here is safe or usable until identity and access are solved.

- Okta SSO authentication — one login per AM, no loose passwords.
- The auth layer in front of our MCP server, so every request ties to a known user.
- The OAuth flow that lets an AM connect in securely.

*Why first:* Identity is the spine everything hangs on…… connectors, permissions, and audit logs are meaningless until we know *who* is making a request.

*Exit gate:* An AM logs in via Okta, hits the tool, and the system knows exactly who they are.

### Phase 1 — Data Foundation: The Database

*The job:* give the agents somewhere to read and write structured data. Like auth, this is a hard prerequisite, not an add-on.

- A lightweight structured data layer (Cloudflare D1) — a single place each client record lives.
- The beginnings of the **unified client record** Jose is picturing.

*Why it matters:* right now there's *nowhere* for the agents to pull structured data from. Until this exists, no skill works reliably. This is the same unified database DR wants — we're just naming it as the foundational phase it has to be.

*Exit gate:* agents can reliably read and write client data.

> Phases 0 and 1 are the foundation. Not glamorous, but the difference between a tool that works and a demo that falls over. Most of the “is this hard?” energy in the original scope lives right here and it's exactly the part that has to be done right.
> 

### Phase 2 — Connectors & Permissions

*The job:* wire up the tools the skills depend on, and define who's allowed to do what.

- **Connectors** to the third-party tools — Webflow, Google Ads, Meta, Basecamp, Sage, Salesforce. Each is a real integration with its own auth, error handling, and ongoing upkeep.
- **Permissions** — a working version of role-based access (admin / manager / AM / read-only). *(To answer the open question: yes, this is absolutely a thing — it's the access-control layer, and it's standard. The MVP stands up a working version; the full four-tier enterprise treatment with formal audit/compliance controls is a later hardening item.)*

*Why sequenced here:* connectors are where the real integration cost lives (~$3k–$10k *per* API at market) and only make sense once auth and the database exist to support them.

*Exit gate:* skills can reach their tools, access is governed by role, and an AM can run a skill end-to-end.

### Phase 3 — The AM Skills (the 10x layer)

*The job:* deliver the capabilities that make this a 10x tool for the AM role — the website builds, SEO, ads, reporting, and client handoff described in the section above.

*Exit gate:* an AM can run each skill on a real client and get a usable result.

### Phase 4 — Evaluation & Implementation: “Is this actually working?”

*The job:* this is the phase that makes the engagement worth it. We don't ship skills and walk away — we measure how AMs actually use them, whether they work, and what's missing. This is the part most teams skip, and it's why most AI pilots quietly die.

*(What we spoke about above.)*

- **Instrumentation on every skill** — success-rate evaluations.
- **Usage analysis** — how are AMs actually using this, and where do they get stuck?
- **Gap surfacing** — what are AMs asking for that the tool can't do yet? That list becomes the roadmap.
- **Iteration** — tighten what underperforms, based on real data.

*Exit gate:* real data on what's working, an adoption signal, and a prioritized list of what to build next enough for a confident scale-or-stop decision.

## The one thing we have to name out loud: 
This is an MVP scope, not an enterprise scope.

We want to be a great partner here, which means being straight with you about something in the follow-up. Reading the additions and Jose's questions together, what's being described — a unified client database tying together Basecamp/Sage/Salesforce, Okta SSO across the org, four role-based permission tiers, audit logging, dead-letter queues, a retry dashboard, documented architecture at 2x scale, formal infrastructure transfer. Is an **enterprise platform spec.** It's all reasonable to *want.* It's just a different animal from the MVP this budget is scoped for.

For context, here's what the market actually charges for the enterprise version of this:

- Custom AI agent development in 2026 generally runs **$65k–$300k+, with most mid-market builds landing $120k–$150k.**
- The specific enterprise tier… the one with SSO, multi-tenant architecture, RBAC, advanced monitoring, and SLA-backed support, is quoted at **$75k–$500k+.**
- Integrations are priced individually: **roughly $3k–$10k per connected API.** This build touches six (Webflow, Google Ads, Meta, Basecamp, Sage, Salesforce), so **$18k–$60k in integration work alone,** before a single skill, the database, SSO, or access tiers.
- Built to the full enterprise spec, year-one all-in for something like this lands around **$160k (lean) to $400k+ (enterprise-grade).**

We're not raising this to renegotiate, we're raising it so expectations and budget line up. **At the current number, this is genuinely a steal: it's below the floor of even a “simple MVP” range, and a fraction of the enterprise build the follow-up describes.** The integrations alone could consume the whole budget at market rate. 

<aside>
💡

(You’ve already started to experience this with Impravado and C-Data and you have ***zero*** platform ownership.)

</aside>

**Where we are at:**

- The MVP delivers the *working tool* — the skills, the database foundation, the eval loop — at the scoped price. That's the part that creates value on day one.
- The enterprise hardening (full SSO rollout, four-tier RBAC, DLQ + retry dashboard, 2x-scale architecture, formal SOC-style controls) is real, valuable work that belongs in **later phases or a follow-on**, priced as what it is.
    - To be very straight with you: a lot of it is built for a different risk profile than yours. Those controls exist for regulated, “high-blast-radius” environments…. finance, healthcare, anything where a failed job or an access slip is a compliance event. For a marketing agency where the worst case is "a site build needs a rerun," much of it is insurance against risks you don't carry.
- The MVP earns the right to that investment by *proving* it on real AM usage — so when you do spend enterprise money, it's backed by data instead of a guess.

The ask: Let's agree on what's in the MVP envelope vs. what's a fast-follow, so nobody expects a $400k platform inside an MVP budget. Naming it now is how we avoid the awkward version of this conversation three weeks into the build.

## On cost.

Everything runs on Anthropic's API, billed per million tokens. The model spend is **nominal.** The real cost of this project is build time and infrastructure (the database, hosting, background workers), not per-call token usage.

Rough per-action estimates at production scale:

| Action | Ballpark cost | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Full Webflow site from scratch | ~$0.40–$1.20 | ~20 min; many background workers running in parallel. Heaviest single action. |
| Google/Meta ad set (brief → variants + reasoning) | a few cents | ~$0.05–$0.10 with caching on |
| Client report (replaces 1–2 days of manual work) | ~$0.10–$0.30 | The killer ROI line — pennies for 1–2 human-days |
| SEO plan (keyword research + site health + 90-day) | ~$0.10–$0.40 | Scales with how much site data we feed in |

Two levers keep this low regardless of volume: **Prompt caching** (up to 90% off repeated input) and the **batch API** (50% off). Combined, up to ~95% savings on the parts that qualify. Non-creative steps (parsing, structure mapping, QA) run on cheaper models; only the creative generation needs the top tier.

**Fixed vs. usage-based:** hosting, the database, and background-worker infrastructure are fixed/predictable. API model usage is usage-based — it scales with how many sites/reports/ads AMs actually generate, which is exactly the kind of cost that tracks value created.

## What it costs to run each month (the all-in number)

Separate from the per-action token cost above, here's the ongoing infrastructure to keep the tool live for the whole AM team. We'd expect this to land in the **$250–$500/month** range all-in, and here's what makes it up:

| Service | What it does | Rough monthly |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cloudflare (Workers, D1 database, hosting, queue) | The core infrastructure — database, background workers, hosting | ~$5–$50 |
| Remote browser layer (for Webflow builds) | The cloud browser sessions that drive Webflow site builds | ~$100–$250 |
| Integration / connector layer (Conductor) | Managed authentication + connections to the third-party tools, prompt caching, batch API | ~$40–$100 |
| Anthropic model usage | The per-action token cost from the table above | Usage-based (see below) |

**The single biggest driver is the remote browser layer for Webflow.** That's not a surprise…. it's the hardest skill doing the most work (20–30 minutes of live cloud-browser time per full site build). It scales with *how many sites get built*, not with headcount, so it tracks real output rather than seat count. We're also evaluating consolidating that browser layer onto Cloudflare directly, which would push the whole monthly number toward the **low end** of the band.

**On the Anthropic model usage specifically:** this is genuinely nominal per action (the per-action table above), and an important nuance for budgeting — **a large portion of it can run through each AM's own Claude plan rather than as a separate bill**, depending on how DR has Claude / Claude Code set up for the team. So the "AI cost" is partly absorbed by seats you may already be paying for. We'll firm up the exact split once we see how your team's Claude access is configured.

The honest takeaway: **for a tool serving your entire AM team, you're looking at roughly the cost of one mid-tier SaaS subscription per month** — and the part that costs the most is the part that does the most, which is building entire websites end-to-end.

## Jose's technical questions

**Ongoing costs at scale (700 clients, 120 employees).** Covered above. Fixed: hosting, DB, workers. Usage-based: API model calls (the per-action table). At your scale the model spend stays nominal per action; caching + batch hold it down as volume grows. (Note: per-token *usage* cost is nominal — that's separate from the *build* cost of the platform itself, which is addressed in the MVP-vs-enterprise-scope section above.)

**Infrastructure ownership.** Yes — written confirmation that DR owns all repos, databases, and infrastructure accounts. Ownership transfers **on final payment** — a single, clean handover once the engagement is paid in full (see the Ownership & Entity section below for the full picture, including why there's no partial transfer along the way). Handoff is documented per component so Jose's team can run and maintain it.

**Bug fixes vs. enhancements.** Standard line: if something we built breaks post-delivery, that's a bug fix and it's included. A *new* capability or a change to agreed behavior is an enhancement ($200/hr). When it's ambiguous, we flag it before doing the work and agree on the call together — no surprise invoices. Important nuance: a third-party API change that takes a skill down (e.g. Meta versions an endpoint) is the kind of ongoing upkeep a maintenance retainer is built to cover — see *“This is a living system, not a website”* below for why that's structurally different from a one-time bug.

**Scalability — 25+ AMs running skills simultaneously.** Two things make this a non-issue, and it's worth separating them. First, the realistic load: it's unrealistic that all 25 AMs fire the same skill in the same second  (actual usage is a handful of overlapping jobs across the day, which the queue absorbs comfortably.) Second, the architecture: Claude itself is a stateless API that scales horizontally on Anthropic's side concurrency is not “25 people sharing one brain.” 

The MCP server is built to handle multiple users at once, authenticating each request and managing each AM's session independently. Long jobs (like a 20-minute site build) run through a background queue rather than blocking anyone. 
So “25 AMs at once” is the design intent, not an edge case. What Phases 3–4 add is *production hardening* for that load — dead-letter queue, retry visibility, and behavior at 2x — not basic multi-user capability, which is there from day one.

**Which jobs run on Cloudflare Workers vs. a separate queue.** Short, fast tasks run on Workers; long-running jobs (e.g. a full site build, ~20 min) go through a queue with background workers. We'll document the split as part of architecture handoff.

**Dead-letter queue / retry dashboard for Jose's team.** — not a day-one MVP deliverable.

**Architecture at 2x scale.** Same answer — we'll document the target architecture, and the MVP's instrumentation gives us the real numbers to size it correctly rather than estimating blind.

**Sensitive data & access controls.** Credentials handled via the OAuth/Okta flow rather than stored loosely; Sage Intacct access governed by role-based tiers (admin / manager / AM / read-only). Audit logging (who ran what and when) is part of the instrumentation we're building anyway. On secure credential storage specifically: where a client's API keys or tokens have to be stored, they're held in a dedicated, encrypted secrets layer, we'd use either **Cloudflare Tunnels + Access** (keeping it inside the same Cloudflare environment as the rest of the stack) or **AWS KMS** (a dedicated, industry-standard key-management service), not loose config or plaintext.

Worth flagging: *full* four-tier RBAC, org-wide SSO rollout, and formal audit/compliance controls are exactly the enterprise-hardening items noted in the scope section above — the MVP stands up the foundation and a working version of access control plus secure credential storage; the full enterprise treatment is a fast-follow. 

<aside>
🔥

***^Again would say this is overkill for your use case. You will waster hundreds (if not) hundreds of thousands chasing a moving target.***

</aside>

## One important architecture note (the MCP / connector point)

Worth flagging because it shapes how every future tool gets added: in Claude, you **can't add two custom connectors that share the same MCP server URL.** So DR connects to **one** Digital Resource MCP server. Employees OAuth into it (Okta sits in front of that flow), and Claude calls the tools using each user's authorized credentials.

The practical consequence: **Future capabilities get added to the same MCP, you can't have duplicate tools across separate connectors.** That's actually a feature, not a limitation it means one governed surface, one place for role-based access, one audit trail. On Team/Enterprise an Owner adds the connector to the org once, then each employee individually connects and enables it, which maps cleanly onto Jose's role-tier requirement.

## How it actually works: Claude vs. MCP vs. Server

*Claude is the brain, our MCP is the hands, Okta is the front door. The brain takes care of itself — the hands are what we maintain.*

## This is a living system, not a website 
(it's not *if* it breaks, it's *when*)

The most important expectation to set before kickoff, so we'll be blunt: **a perfectly built version of this tool will still go down sometimes** (not because of bad work) but because it depends on systems nobody in this room controls. Two ways that happens, both routine:

**When an AI provider has an outage, the AI skills pause.** Claude runs on Anthropic's infrastructure; when that has a bad day, the thinking layer is unavailable until it recovers — same as every AI tool on the market. 

- Not theoretical: Anthropic had **major outages on April 7, 15, and 28, 2026** — the April 28 one took down [Claude.ai](http://Claude.ai), Claude Code, *and* the API at once, with 12,000+ user reports. Their own status page shows the API at **~99% uptime over the trailing 90 days** genuinely good, and also a few hours a year where requests fail. The tool self-recovers when the provider does, but during the window someone needs to be monitoring so AMs know what's happening instead of assuming it's “broken.”

**When a third-party vendor changes their API, that skill breaks until we patch it and this is *scheduled*, not random:**

- **Google Ads API v20 sunsets June 10, 2026** — after that, requests on the old version fail instantly. (v19 already sunset this past February.) Google now ships versions monthly, so it's a recurring upgrade treadmill.
- **Meta deprecated Detailed Targeting interests as of January 15, 2026** — ad sets using them stopped running. Meta's v25 shipped breaking changes across the board; teams routinely report **2–4 weeks of work** on Meta migrations billed as “minor updates.”

That's two of our six connectors with *known, dated* breaking changes (the other four behave the same way. So a skill going dark one Tuesday because Google sunset a version isn't a sign something went wrong; it's the normal lifecycle of building on live platforms.)

**This is why AI agent work is a build fee *plus* a monthly maintenance retainer or. dedicated in-house person maintaining** — covering monitoring, incident response, fixing API connections when vendors change them, and re-tuning skills as models evolve. A common planning benchmark is **10–15% of annual platform cost** for upkeep. The build gets it working; there needs to be some form of maintenance. The question was never “will this break?”… it's “when it breaks, who's watching and how fast does it come back?” That's what production-grade actually means, and it's exactly why doing this *truly* production-grade at the scale the original scope describes is hard and ongoing, not a one-time deliverable.

## Ownership & Entity

The follow-up raised ownership a few times ((including making sure everything lands with DR and not with “WorkMade” )so let's be completely clear, because we don't want any ambiguity here before kickoff.

**Who you're working with.** Your contracting entity is **Quarter Two**, the consultancy delivering this engagement. **WorkMade is a separate consumer-product company with no involvement in or affiliation with this project whatsoever.** It isn't a party to this work, doesn't touch your build, and has no claim to anything here. If WorkMade came up anywhere, it can be set aside entirely this is a Quarter Two engagement, start to finish.

**What DR owns.** Everything we build for you and everything specific to Digital Resource is **yours**:

- Your custom skills, orchestrations, and workflows
- Your data and unified client records
- Your build standards and configurations
- The website builds themselves
- All repos, databases, and infrastructure accounts (formally transferred on final payment).

That's the part with real, lasting value — the custom layer built specifically for DR — and it's 100% yours.

**When ownership transfers.** Ownership of all of the above transfers **on final payment** once the engagement is paid in full, everything (repos, databases, infrastructure accounts, and all custom work) is formally handed over to DR. To be clear and avoid any confusion: there's **no partial or staged ownership transfer along the way.** Quarter Two carries and operates the build through delivery; the full handover happens as a single, clean transfer when the final invoice is settled. This is standard, and it protects both sides (you get a complete, documented handover in one piece rather than a half-owned system mid-build.)

**What no one “owns” — because it's third-party platform underneath.** The custom layer is built on top of platforms that everyone in the industry rents and no single company owns — the cloud infrastructure (Cloudflare), the managed integration layer, and the AI models (Anthropic). These aren't things we keep from you; they're things *nobody* owns, the same way you don't “own” the cloud provider or the power grid your office runs on. The important part for you: **you hold your own accounts and direct access to each of these.** No vendor lock-in, no hostage situation, nothing routed through us that you can't reach yourself.

**The simple version:** you own everything that's yours and hold your own keys to everything underneath. Quarter Two builds it, hands it over, and (if you want us) maintains it. Nobody's keeping anything from you; this is just how the stack works.

## On the sequencing request

Front-loading a visible SEO/content/ads win in weeks 3–6 alongside the Webflow work: totally reasonable, and we're happy to prioritize whichever skill is simplest to stand up first so you get an early internal win. Noted as a priority preference, not a scope change.

## **Website cloning, why it's out of scope**

We want to flag this directly because it sounds like a small addition and absolutely is not. 

Cloning an existing site  (pointing the tool at someone's live WordPress site and having it faithfully rebuild in Webflow is a fundamentally harder problem than building a new site from scratch.

Building *new* sites works because it's a **repeatable workflow**: we control the starting point, the structure, the template. AI is exceptional at repeatable workflows with known variables that's exactly where it shines. For context, the Webflow build skill we already have took us **over a month of engineering to reach ~90% fidelity** and that's the *easy* direction, where we control the inputs.

Cloning flips that. Every source site is built differently…. different structure, CMS quirks, custom code, one-off layouts, broken markup, assets scattered everywhere. ***(And the assumption the site was built properly.)*** The variables change on every single job, so there's no clean repeatable process to lean on. That raises the real question worth asking on any build like this: **is this a software problem, an AI problem, or a combination of both?** Cloning is squarely the messy combination and that's where cost and effort climb fast, because you're handling endless edge cases instead of running one reliable pattern.

It's *doable.* The honest questions are "at what cost?" and "what level of 'done' is good enough? because a clone that's 80% right often creates more cleanup than building fresh. So we're keeping it out of this scope deliberately. If it becomes a real need, it's its own scoped project, priced for what it actually is.

For perspective: **If we'd quoted the website-builder skill on its own, we'd have priced it at $35K alone** that's how intense a build it was. The only reason it's folded into this engagement instead of its own line item is that we already built it with y’all. Cloning would be a comparable undertaking from zero. We'd rather hand you a working builder we've already invested in than sell you a cloning project that eats the budget and frustrates everyone.

## Bottom line

We're in, and we're excited. Everything listed is the right direction. The one ask back is that we all treat v1 as what it is: a focused, instrumented, production-ready MVP built for the account-manager role and scoped for your AM team whose real output is *learning*: what works, what AMs reach for, and where to invest next. The database comes first because nothing works without it. And let's align on the MVP envelope vs. the enterprise fast-follow, so the scope and the budget tell the same story.

Worth repeating the part we're proudest of: The discovery and R&D that usually *starts* an engagement like this (and usually gets billed) is already done, on us. So we're not starting from a blank page on your budget. We have a plan, we've pressure-tested the architecture, and we can start executing on day one.

As always, happy to hop on a call to walk through any of this live.
